name: Agones
summary: Runs dedicated multiplayer game servers on Kubernetes: keeps a fleet of them warm, hands one to each match, and never kills a server while players are on it.
intro: A dedicated game server is an odd workload. It holds a whole match in memory, lives for minutes or hours rather than months, and players connect straight to its IP address and port, because a load balancer would add latency and split players who must share one simulation. Agones teaches Kubernetes about this with custom resources and a controller. A `GameServer` is a Pod plus a host port (picked dynamically by default) and a lifecycle state; a `Fleet` keeps a number of them warm, with rolling updates; a `FleetAutoscaler` keeps a buffer of `Ready` servers above however many are in use.

The flow follows a match. The game server process calls the Agones SDK’s `Ready()` once it can take players. A matchmaker then creates a `GameServerAllocation`, which atomically picks a `Ready` server matching its filters, marks it `Allocated` and returns its address and port. Allocated servers are left alone by scale-down and fleet updates until the process calls `Shutdown()` at the end of the match. The SDK is a thin client for a sidecar that Agones runs next to each server, with versions for Unreal Engine, Unity, C++, Go, C#, Node.js and Rust, plus a REST interface.

Google and Ubisoft announced Agones in March 2018, and it lives in Google’s `googleforgames` organisation on GitHub. Version 1.0 shipped in September 2019, and in 2026 it put out a minor release about every six weeks. Google Cloud also sold Agones as a managed service, Game Servers (beta in March 2020, generally available that August), but that product has been retired: its documentation now redirects to Google Cloud’s games page, which points to Agones itself.
strengths: Purpose-built lifecycle: warm fleets, atomic allocation, and no scale-down or rollout of servers with players on them
Game servers and the services around them (accounts, inventory, matchmaking) run on one platform with standard Kubernetes tools
Runs wherever Kubernetes runs: any cloud, on-premises, or a developer laptop
Mature and steadily released: version 1.0 in 2019 and a minor release roughly every six weeks
limits: Players connect directly to node IPs and host ports, so nodes need public addresses and open port ranges
It allocates servers but doesn’t match players: you bring a matchmaker (Google’s Open Match is one option)
An Allocated server is only removed when the game calls `Shutdown()` (or someone deletes it), so a server that never exits keeps holding capacity
The managed Google Cloud Game Servers offering is gone, so you operate the cluster and Agones yourself

snippet.title: A fleet of warm game servers, then an allocation for one match
source: replicas: 10            # GameServers kept Ready or Allocated
scheduling: Packed      # bin-pack, so empty nodes can be removed
portPolicy: Dynamic   # Agones picks a free host port
kind: GameServerAllocation   # created by the matchmaker per match

story: Fast-paced online games such as shooters, MOBAs and MMOs need a dedicated server that runs the authoritative copy of each match. Studios usually built their own systems to start, place and scale those servers, because general orchestrators assumed long-running, load-balanced services, not short-lived stateful processes that players connect to directly.

Google Cloud and Ubisoft announced Agones on March 13, 2018, its name coming from the Greek for “contest” or “gathering”. Instead of a separate game server manager, it extended Kubernetes with a GameServer resource and a controller, so any matchmaker could request a server through the Kubernetes API. The first release, v0.1, was an alpha; Fleets were the next feature planned.

Version 1.0 arrived in September 2019. In 2020 Google Cloud launched Game Servers, a managed service built on Agones, but the product was later retired, leaving the open-source project as the way to use it.

choices.choice: Extend Kubernetes rather than build a new scheduler
choices.why: Studios could run game servers and their supporting services on one platform, reuse Kubernetes tooling and the work of its contributors, and run it anywhere from a laptop to multiple clouds.

choices.choice: Direct IP and port, no load balancer
choices.why: Players in a match share one in-memory simulation and are sensitive to latency, so they connect straight to the server process; Agones allocates host ports and reports the address back.

choices.choice: An SDK inside the game server
choices.why: Only the game knows when it is ready for players, healthy, or finished. The SDK reports those moments, so Agones never removes a server mid-match.

choices.choice: Allocation as an atomic API call
choices.why: Two matchmakers must never get the same server. A GameServerAllocation picks a Ready server and marks it Allocated in one step.
